clue.text: Son is trapped by a stone - help

indicators.note: whatever is trapped is held inside something else, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son
taken as written
taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight

explanation.surface: A boy stuck under a fallen rock cries out for help.
explanation.walkthrough: The son and 'is' join up and are trapped inside the stone abbreviation, with A leading. A stone is 14 pounds in British weights.
explanation.definitionFit: To assist is to give aid or support, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Where piles are stored: small shabby area requiring drastic service primarily

indicators.note: what comes primarily comes first, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
tacky means cheap and shabby
the initial letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A run-down little yard in urgent need of repair.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'area' look like part of the description, but it opens the run of initials. S + TACKY + ARDS gives STACKYARDS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stackyard is a farm enclosure where hay or corn stacks are kept, so piles of harvested crops sit there.

clue.text: Not quite mature solver’s silence after swilling gin

indicators.note: swilling sloshes liquid round, so these letters are swirled into a new order

blocks.note: the solver is addressed as 'you' in crosswords; the possessive just attaches the next piece
taken as written, then rearranged
SH is the call for silence

explanation.surface: A slightly immature crossword solver goes quiet after knocking back some gin.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords address the solver as 'you', and the possessive simply glues the next piece on; 'after' places the silence last.
explanation.definitionFit: Youngish means fairly young, so someone described that way is still some distance from full maturity.

clue.text: Contributor to garden in every square

indicators.note: a contributor supplies a part of the whole, so the letters are part of the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone who helps look after the garden in every town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' reads as a town square in the surface, but it is the mathematical sense: gardeN IN Every.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine equals three multiplied by itself, making it a perfect square number in arithmetic.

clue.text: Eating nuts?

blocks.note: first meaning: away having a midday meal
second meaning: slightly crazy, in slang

explanation.surface: Someone snacking on a handful of nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests eating nuts as food; instead the two words are separate senses of one phrase, one literal and one slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally describes someone away for a midday meal, and informally describes someone who is crazy or not all there.

clue.text: New bits of music having no power for relatives

indicators.note: having none of something means it has been taken out, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
pieces are musical compositions
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: Fresh compositions played without electricity at a family gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: N + PIECES with the P removed gives N + IECES.
explanation.definitionFit: Nieces are the daughters of one's siblings, and so family members or kin.

clue.text: Raised end of wood beam from which sail hangs

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the spar

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept
in a down clue, raising letters makes them read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the final letter of this word
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A wooden beam lifted up on a ship to carry the sail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wood beam' looks like a single thing, but the words split: D + RAY makes DRAY, which reads upwards as YARD.
explanation.definitionFit: On a square-rigged ship the spar slung across the mast, supporting a sail, is called a yard.

clue.text: Obscure reply not about abuse

indicators.note: 'not' excludes something, so the next item is taken out

blocks.note: to mist something is to obscure it
to react is to respond
C is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A vague response that avoids addressing a complaint of abuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' looks like an adjective describing the reply, but it is a verb giving MIST. REACT loses C, the abbreviation circa, to give REAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To mistreat someone is to handle them badly or cruelly, a direct verb synonym.

clue.text: Group closed dispute

blocks.note: a set is a group
a door pushed to is closed

explanation.surface: A clique that shuts down an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: TO as closed comes from the phrase 'push the door to', meaning shut it.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is an informal word for a quarrel or fight, so it matches a dispute.

clue.text: Opera - pair in it flailing around for all to see

indicators.note: flailing limbs thrash about wildly, so the letters are thrown into disorder
going around something encloses it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
U is the film certificate meaning suitable for everyone

explanation.surface: Two opera singers thrashing about on stage in full view of the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: PAIRINIT is rearranged as IPRITANI and wrapped around U, the British film rating for universal viewing.
explanation.definitionFit: I Puritani is an opera by Vincenzo Bellini, first performed in Paris in 1835.

clue.text: Performing, still to accept study offered by college

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: inert means motionless
to con is to study, an old word
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A college course on performance that you are still due to take up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con' is an old verb meaning to study or learn by heart; with the college letter it sits inside the word for still.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians in concert are giving a live show on stage, so they are performing.

clue.text: Private eye recalled apprehending a daughter and younger son

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters come back in reverse order
apprehending is seizing and holding, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a tec is an informal word for a detective
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A detective remembered arresting a girl and her little brother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' sounds like memory, but it turns the detective back to front before the pair goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage a cadet is a son other than the eldest, a junior branch of a family.

clue.text: DNA chemical no longer for you and for me

blocks.note: thy is the archaic form of 'your', belonging to you
mine means belonging to me

explanation.surface: A chemical in DNA that is now obsolete, split between you and me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' marks an archaic word: THY is old-fashioned 'your', followed by MINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thymine is one of the four nucleotide bases found in DNA, pairing with adenine.

clue.text: It’s Y - no more arguments

definitions.note: cryptic: the letter at the close of a word

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: the final letter of the word in question
second meaning: a phrase closing a discussion

explanation.surface: Someone asked why, answering 'because I said so' to shut down debate.
explanation.walkthrough: Y sounds like 'why', inviting a question, but it is simply the last letter of STORY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said to declare that a matter is settled and there is nothing further to discuss.

clue.text: Way to include spinach in Italian dish

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a lane is a way or road
sag, or saag, is spinach in Indian cooking

explanation.surface: A method for getting spinach into a pasta bake.
explanation.walkthrough: Spinach comes from Indian cooking, as in the curry-house side dish sag aloo, and sits inside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasagne is the baked Italian pasta dish of layered sheets, sauce and cheese.

clue.text: Fault-finder upset about a university accepting dodgy grant on a big scale

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting letters tips them over so they read upwards
something dodgy is unreliable and out of order, so the letters are jumbled
going about something surrounds it, so one piece encloses another
accepting means taking in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a nag constantly criticises
taken as written
taken as written, then rearranged
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A critic angry that a university has taken a questionable grant of enormous size.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest here: the scrambled grant sits between A and the university, and the upturned critic wraps round the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Gargantuan means enormous, after Rabelais's giant Gargantua, so it describes things on a huge scale.

clue.text: Hard to abandon cleaner vehicle

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
a char is a cleaning lady, short for charwoman

explanation.surface: It is difficult to walk away from a cleaning van.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is an old British term for a woman paid to clean houses. CHAR loses H.
explanation.definitionFit: A car is a motor vehicle for carrying passengers on roads.

clue.text: Prize given to one song that’s depicted heartless greed

indicators.note: without a heart means the centre is gone, so the middle letter is removed

blocks.note: a cup is a trophy
I is the Roman numeral for one
a ditty is a short simple song

explanation.surface: An award handed to a song portraying a cold, grasping character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless greed' reads as one phrase, but 'heartless' applies to the song: DITTY loses its central T.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupidity is an eager desire for wealth or possessions, a formal word for avarice.

clue.text: Male academic I see pursuing pleasure

blocks.note: he is a male person
a don is a university teacher
I as written, and C for 'see' since the letter is pronounced that way

explanation.surface: A professor admits he spots a colleague chasing enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is an Oxford or Cambridge lecturer. The letter C is said the same as 'see'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hedonic relates to pleasure-seeking, as in hedonism, the pursuit of enjoyment as life's goal.

clue.text: Ornamental planter caught with long lid upended

indicators.note: turned end over end, so in a down entry the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
to ache for something is to long for it
a top is a lid

explanation.surface: A decorative flowerpot snagged by its long lid being flipped over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' seems to describe the lid, but it is a verb giving ACHE; TOP flips to POT.
explanation.definitionFit: A cachepot is a decorative container used to hold and hide a plain flowerpot.

clue.text: Conservative not fully reversing corruption

indicators.note: something not fully present is incomplete, so its last letter is cut
going into reverse means travelling backwards, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A half-hearted Tory backtracking on a corruption scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: TORY without its last letter is TOR, which turns round to ROT.
explanation.definitionFit: Rot means decay or moral decline, so it serves as a synonym of corruption.

clue.text: Launch promotion about exhibition, having taken week away

indicators.note: taking something away removes it, here a single abbreviated letter
being about something is surrounding it, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a puff is a piece of publicity
a show is an exhibition

explanation.surface: A publicity campaign for an exhibition that has been cut by a week.
explanation.walkthrough: W is the abbreviation for week, so SHOW becomes SHO, which sits inside PUFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A push-off is the shove that starts a boat moving from the bank, hence a start or launch.

clue.text: Marine creature only gutted on rear of vessel? Not entirely

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, so just the outer letters survive
not the entire thing means one letter is missing from the end

blocks.note: the first and last letters of this word
the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: A sea creature cleaned out on the back deck of a ship, though not completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and 'Not entirely' seem to comment on the whole scene, but they only trim STERN to STER.
explanation.definitionFit: An oyster is a bivalve mollusc living in the sea, a clear example of sea life.

clue.text: Court brought in auditor, disposing of last parcel of land

indicators.note: something brought in is taken inside, so one piece sits within another
getting rid of the final item means the end letter is cut

blocks.note: CT is the abbreviation for court
an auditor is a listener, someone who hears

explanation.surface: A court calls in a financial auditor to handle the sale of the final plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests accounts, but in its older Latin-rooted sense it means a listener, one who hears.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectare is a metric unit of land area, ten thousand square metres, so it names a plot.

clue.text: Each old coin about right for jewellery item

blocks.note: EA is the abbreviation for each
R is the abbreviation for right
a bob was a shilling in pre-decimal British money

explanation.surface: Each antique coin is about the right price for a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: A bob was slang for the shilling, a coin in British money before 1971. R sits against BOB.
explanation.definitionFit: An earbob is a dangling earring, an item of jewellery worn on the ear.

clue.text: French composer’s unhappy, reflecting about another European country

indicators.note: a reflection is a mirror image, so the letters appear backwards
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: sad means unhappy
the United Kingdom, another country in Europe

explanation.surface: A French composer is miserable, brooding on a rival nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' European country, because France is already in the clue, so Britain is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Dukas was a French composer, best known for The Sorcerer's Apprentice.

clue.text: Part of body that’s been kneaded partially after twisting

indicators.note: partially means in part, so only a portion of the words is used
twisting round turns a thing about, so the letters read the other way

blocks.note: read backwards across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A limb that has been massaged after a painful twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kneaded' looks like it should sound the answer, but the letters run backwards through beEN Kneaded.
explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the joint in the middle of the leg, a part of the human body.

clue.text: Something that really distresses blokes between high points

indicators.note: sitting between two things means being flanked by them, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop, and the plural gives two of them
blokes is British slang for men

explanation.surface: Something upsetting that keeps men stuck between mountain peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hill, common on Dartmoor; the plural 'points' gives two, with MEN placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tormentor is one who causes severe suffering or anguish, which fits a source of deep distress.

clue.text: Run time rising? Not often

definitions.note: adverbial phrase for an adjective, as in 'visits are not often'

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters go upwards, reading back to front

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone asking if it is time to go jogging, answered: hardly ever.
explanation.walkthrough: R, then ERA reading upwards as ARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare happens seldom or infrequently, so it does not occur often.

clue.text: Heroin during new year festival a mistake, producing horrific persecution

indicators.note: something happening during an event falls within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: Tet is the Vietnamese lunar new year
H is slang for heroin
an error is a mistake; the article is absorbed

explanation.surface: Drug-taking at a new year celebration was a blunder that led to a brutal crackdown.
explanation.walkthrough: The festival is the Vietnamese lunar new year, not the Western one; the drug goes inside it before the mistake follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Terror was the period of mass executions during the French Revolution, 1793 to 1794.

clue.text: New Zealand region identified in ancient texts in the past

blocks.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of ancient scriptures
ago means in the past

explanation.surface: A New Zealand region that historians find named in old manuscripts.
explanation.walkthrough: OT for Old Testament is a standard crossword abbreviation, then AGO.
explanation.definitionFit: Otago is a region in the south of New Zealand's South Island, containing Dunedin.
